paras: The lynching of J. D. Mayfield took place in Danville, Illinois, on the night of July 25, 1903, when a white mob seized a Black man held for the fatal shooting of Henry Gatterman, a white butcher, hanged him from a pole and burned his body before the county jail. The mob then besieged the jail to lynch a second Black prisoner, James Wilson, until Sheriff H. H. Whitlock and his deputies fired into it. A coroner's jury blamed persons unknown, but twelve members of the jail mob went to prison, and both presses held up the sheriff as a model.

Wilson was in the county jail, charged with assaulting Mrs. Thomas Burgess, a farmer's wife at nearby Alvin, and the wire said he had confessed. One Indianapolis Journal correspondent traced the outbreak to resentment of a new city administration that had given jail-guard posts and a fire company to Black men.

According to the Associated Press, a crowd marching to lynch Wilson quarreled with a Black man from Evansville, Indiana, who fired into it and killed Gatterman. The Indianapolis Journal's correspondent and the Plymouth Tribune instead placed a saloon quarrel first, the Plymouth paper calling the attempt on Wilson "an afterthought."

Officers barricaded him in the city building, but the mob battered through the door. The Indianapolis Journal said police admitted part of the crowd, which dragged him from a vault, beat him and shot him. The mob dragged him to the scene of the shooting, hanged him from a pole and riddled the body with bullets, then carried it to the square before the jail and burned it. Men fired into the flames and hacked the corpse, cutting off the ears.

Whitlock told the crowd that Wilson "has not been identified as the man who assaulted Mrs. Burgess," but it rammed the jail door with a rail. The sheriff, deputies and a Black turnkey fired a volley; the crowd then stoned the jail and sent for dynamite, which citizens intercepted. It dispersed about 2:15 a.m., and three to four other Black men, one named as Ben Rich, were reported beaten.

Four companies of the Seventh Illinois Infantry arrived, and Black residents left the city by interurban car. At the inquest few witnesses would admit being present, and the verdict was death at the hands of persons unknown.

Arrests followed, among them Winfield Baker, called the mob's leader, and Bessie Armstrong, or Dodge, accused of urging the crowd to shoot the sheriff. Wilson was indicted on August 3 and sentenced on his confession within two hours. The Cleveland Gazette noted that the indictments covered the jail attack, and that the names of those who lynched Mayfield had not been obtained. On September 6 a jury convicted twelve jail rioters after Richard Roberts turned state's evidence, and in November 1904 the pardon board refused to cut their five-year sentences.

The first wire announced that "A race war has broken out" and called the victim an "unidentified negro refugee from Evansville"; later reports named him Mayfield or Metcalf. The Indianapolis Journal called him "a big, burly negro," and the Rock Island Argus headlined "Black Scoundrel Precipitates Reign of Terror." In Mississippi the Hattiesburg Daily Progress said such a man "is lynched—hanged in the south and burned in the north."

Black weeklies carried the wire from July 31, the Professional World under "Negro Lynched and Burned at Stake." The Chicago Broad-Ax wrote its own account, calling it "Anarchy, mob and lynch law" and blaming the mayor, the police and Governor Yates. It conceded that Mayfield "had no right to shoot Henry Gatterman" and called for an Illinois anti-lynching law like Ohio's. The Indianapolis Freeman wrote that "Metcalf had a gun" and urged Black men not to carry weapons.
On the sheriff the presses converged: the Iowa Bystander reprinted white editorials praising Whitlock, and the St. Paul Appeal offered "All honor."

The wire said Mayfield was hanged alive, the Indianapolis Journal that he was shot first, and a closing Tribune paragraph that he was found in a safe and stamped to death. Estimates of the mob ran from 600 to over four thousand, and of its wounded from three to "more than twenty."

bases: A mob took a Black man accused of killing a white man from officers in the city building, hanged him, shot into his body and burned it (A2, A3, A39), then besieged the county jail to lynch a second Black prisoner (A9, A34).

A mob reported at 600 or more seized Mayfield from police and killed him by hanging and/or shooting for the killing of Gatterman (A1, A2, A3); a coroner's jury found he died at the hands of persons unknown (A22, A41).

The AP wire (A2, A39), the Indianapolis Journal's special correspondent (A3), the Plymouth Tribune (A17) and the Chicago Broad-Ax (A32, A33) independently agree that a mob seized the man from the city building, hanged him and burned his body, though they differ on details of the killing.

accounts.label: AP wire
accounts.gist: A mob marching to lynch Wilson met Mayfield, who fired into it and killed Gatterman; officers took him to the city building, the mob battered in, hanged him alive on a telephone pole, later burned the body, then attacked the jail and was fired on.

accounts.label: Indianapolis Journal special correspondent
accounts.gist: Metcalf argued with Gatterman before any mob formed and shot him; police admitted part of the crowd, which dragged him from a records vault, beat and shot him in the station, then hanged and burned the body.

accounts.label: Plymouth Tribune 'true story'
accounts.gist: Metcalf shot Gatterman twice after a saloon quarrel over 'the race problem'; the mob formed afterward and the attack on Wilson was an afterthought.

accounts.label: Tribune variant paragraph
accounts.gist: The negro was found hidden in a safe in the wrecked city prison, stamped to death, dragged to the scene of the shooting, and burned after a rope broke.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Chicago Broad-Ax)
accounts.gist: Mayfield was refused a drink and shot Gatterman; Mayor Beard and the police let a mob of over four thousand into the city hall; the body was hanged, shot, kicked and burned before 'Christian' spectators.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Mayfield died at the hands of persons unknown.

framing.detail: First wires called it a 'race war' and identified the victim only as an 'unidentified negro refugee from Evansville' who had killed a member of the mob.
The Indianapolis Journal called the victim 'a big, burly negro' and 'the murderer' while headlining the sheriff's 'deadly volley' and blaming Black appointments for the outbreak.
The Rock Island Argus headlined 'Black Scoundrel Precipitates Reign of Terror' over its casualty list.
The Hattiesburg Daily Progress used the riot to say Illinois was no different from Mississippi in lynching Black men.
Northern editorials reprinted in the Black press praised Whitlock and blamed the 'recessant mayor'.
The Chicago Broad-Ax called it 'Anarchy, mob and lynch law', mocked the mob's 'respectable citizens', and attacked the mayor and Gov. Yates.
The Indianapolis Freeman said 'Metcalf had a gun' and urged better Black conduct while denying the mob any excuse.
The St. Paul Appeal, Cleveland Gazette and Rising Son praised Whitlock and the convictions and called the mob 'color-prejudiced'.

info: Saturday night, July 25, 1903; the jail siege lasted until about 2:15 a.m. on July 26
East Main Street near a saloon (shooting and hanging), the city building/police station, and the public square in front of the Vermilion County jail, Danville

J. D. Mayfield (also John D. Mayfield, W. D. Mayfield, John D./J. D. Metcalf, James Metcalf), a Black man said to be from Evansville, Ind., lynched; three to four or more other Black men beaten, one named as Ben Rich

Mayfield was accused of shooting and killing Henry Gatterman, a young white butcher; the mob's original target, James Wilson, was charged with assaulting (or attempting to assault) Mrs. Thomas Burgess at Alvin
A white mob of Danville people; reports say a delegation from Alvin took part in the jail attack; those convicted for the jail attack were mostly miners or laborers, led by Winfield Baker of Kentucky

Wilson sentenced to a long prison term; Bessie Dodge and ten men given indeterminate terms at Chester, Thomas Bell sent to Pontiac; four who pleaded guilty fined $200; pardon board refused to reduce sentences in Nov. 1904; no prosecution for Mayfield's killing reported
